title: Forty Hours on a Bus, Thirteen Visas Denied, Zero Tickets for Fans. Iran Made It to the World Cup Anyway.
excerpt: The Iranian team's journey to the 2026 FIFA World Cup — from Tehran to Tijuana, through a war zone and diplomatic minefield — is the most extraordinary in tournament history.
body:
They took a 40-hour bus ride from Tehran to the Turkish border. Their goalkeeper slept on the floor because at six-foot-five, Alireza Beiranvand could not stretch out in a seat. Thirteen members of their delegation — analysts, media officials, the team manager — were denied American visas. Their ticket allocation was revoked days before the tournament. And when they finally arrived at their World Cup base, it was not in the United States, where their matches will be played, but across the border in Tijuana, Mexico.

Iran's journey to the 2026 FIFA World Cup is unlike anything the tournament has seen in its 96-year history. For the first time, a host nation is receiving a country it is actively at war with. This unprecedented situation casts a long shadow, particularly for the Iranian diaspora in North America, who find themselves navigating a complex mix of national pride, political dissent, and emotional turmoil as their team competes under extraordinary circumstances.

## A Route No Team Has Ever Taken

The squad left Tehran on buses, enduring a punishing overland crossing to Turkey before regrouping in Antalya. From there, they flew to Tijuana via a route that would have been unthinkable under normal circumstances. The original plan — a pre-tournament training camp in Tucson, Arizona — was scrapped after the United States and Israel launched strikes against Iran on February 28, triggering a war that is now in its fourth month.

"They always say once you get off the plane and you enter the host country, there's just a unique atmosphere of friendliness and global-ness," Iran forward Mehdi Taremi told ESPN from Tijuana. "Unfortunately, I'm not feeling it right now."

Taremi, who plays for Inter Milan and is participating in his third World Cup, said the usual camaraderie of the tournament feels absent. "There's a lot of tension right now in this World Cup. You feel it in the atmosphere."

## Visa Denials, Ticket Revocations, and a 'Pride Match' Dispute

While all 26 players and head coach Amir Ghalenoei were granted US visas — issued just 10 days before Iran's first match — several officials were not. The American administration denied entry to 13 delegation members, citing security concerns. Andrew Giuliani, executive director of the White House FIFA task force, said the denials targeted individuals who "may not be coaches" and those with suspected ties to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
